course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Cold War and Decolonization
unit.description: Study how the Cold War divided the world, how colonies won independence, how new states and movements challenged established power, and why the Cold War ended.

questions.prompt: The US-backed overthrow of Guatemala's government in 1954 is best understood in the context of
choices: Cold War fears that land reform would lead to communism
the Spanish conquest of the Americas
Guatemala's decision to join the Warsaw Pact

choices: relied on peasants rather than factory workers

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 8.4 key concept: the Chinese Communist Party won the civil war and transformed China's society and economy
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the Chinese Communist Revolution, 1927–1962
stimulusBlocks.text:
After 1927, China's Nationalist government under Chiang Kai-shek fought the Chinese Communist Party. The Communists, led by Mao Zedong, built support among peasants by promising land, and they gained strength resisting the Japanese invasion. In 1949 Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China, and the Nationalists fled to Taiwan.

The new government seized land from landlords and redistributed it, then organized peasants into collective farms. In 1958 Mao launched the Great Leap Forward to industrialize rapidly. Unrealistic production targets and the diversion of farm labor caused a famine that killed tens of millions of people.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that the famine of the Great Leap Forward was caused mainly by
choices: foreign invasion
government policies
a decline in China's population
the return of land to landlords
questions.explanation: Unrealistic targets and diverted labor were policy choices.
choiceExplanations: There was no invasion in 1958.
Unrealistic targets and diverted labor were policy choices.
Population loss was the result, not the cause.
Land was collectivized.
questions.distinguisher: Deaths reduced the population; they did not cause the famine.

questions.prompt: The proclamation of the People's Republic of China in 1949 is best understood in the context of
choices: the end of the Cold War and the Soviet collapse
the Opium Wars and the unequal treaties
the fall of the Qing dynasty and the warlord era

questions.prompt: According to the passage, Árbenz's land reform included
choices: redistributing unused land, some owned by a US company
selling public land to the United Fruit Company
nationalizing the sugar mills and oil refineries of Cuba
returning land to descendants of Spanish colonial families
questions.explanation: The reform affected United Fruit Company property.
choiceExplanations: The reform affected United Fruit Company property.
The reform took unused land from United Fruit rather than selling land to it.
Castro, not Árbenz, nationalized Cuban mills.
Spanish rule had ended long before.
questions.distinguisher: Nationalizing sugar mills describes Cuba under Castro, not Guatemala.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 8.4 key concept: movements to redistribute land and resources developed in Asia, Africa, and Latin America, sometimes drawing Cold War intervention
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing land reform movements in Latin America, 1952–1961
stimulusBlocks.text:
In Latin America, a small number of families and foreign companies owned much of the best land. In 1952, Guatemala's elected president Jacobo Árbenz began to redistribute unused land, including property of the US-owned United Fruit Company. In 1954 a coup backed by the US Central Intelligence Agency overthrew him.

In Cuba, Fidel Castro's revolutionaries took power in 1959. They seized large estates and nationalized US-owned sugar mills and oil refineries. When the United States cut off trade, Castro turned to the Soviet Union for aid and declared Cuba a socialist state.

questions.prompt: The events in Guatemala and Cuba described in the passage were similar in that
choices: both governments joined the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact alliance
both reforms were quickly reversed by US-backed coups
both governments took land and clashed with US interests
both revolutions were led by Jacobo Árbenz of Guatemala
questions.explanation: Both seized land, and both conflicted with US businesses and policy.
choiceExplanations: Neither joined the Warsaw Pact.
Castro stayed in power.
Both seized land, and both conflicted with US businesses and policy.
Castro led Cuba's revolution.
questions.distinguisher: The coup reversed reform only in Guatemala; Castro survived.

questions.prompt: The passage would best support which argument about land reform in Latin America?
choices: The United States consistently supported land reform
Land inequality had little effect on Latin American politics
Cold War rivalry shaped responses to land reform in Latin America
Latin American revolutions were led by the Soviet Union
questions.explanation: US opposition and Soviet aid both followed from Cold War concerns.

Land inequality drove both movements.
US opposition and Soviet aid both followed from Cold War concerns.
